items: 1Write and enter formulas correctly in a worksheet cell — starting with =, + or - — and understand what actually gets stored in the cell.
2Reference cells and ranges by pointing or typing, and explain why formulas recalculate automatically when their referenced cells change.
3Distinguish relative, absolute and mixed references (B10, $B$10, $B10, B$10), predict how each behaves when a formula is copied, and use F4 to cycle between them.
4Reference other worksheets and use 3-D references (e.g. Sheet1:Sheet4!$D$1:$D$10), and avoid circular references.

6Name cells and ranges using the Name Box, the Formulas tab, and the Name Manager, following the naming rules.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Formula An equation that performs a calculation on the values in a worksheet. What is stored — and shown — in the cell is the result of the formula, not the formula's text; the formula itself is visible in the Formula Bar whenever that cell is selected. Formulas replace the need to compute values by hand or on a calculator and re-type the answer.

Cell reference (cell address) A way of referring to the contents of a single cell or a range of cells in a formula, e.g. B10 or B4:D4, instead of typing the value itself. The Name Box (top-left of the worksheet) always shows the address of the currently active cell.

Operator A symbol that specifies the type of calculation to perform between operands in a formula — e.g. + for addition or & for joining text. Excel groups operators into four categories: arithmetic, comparison, text concatenation and reference.

Circular reference Occurs when a formula refers, directly or indirectly, back to its own cell — e.g. entering =(D1+D2-D3)/3 inside cell D3. Circular references should be avoided; the spreadsheet cannot resolve them.
Named range A meaningful word or label (e.g. Sales) that stands in for a cell or range address (e.g. B2:B12), making formulas easier to read and maintain.

sections.title: What a formula cell actually stores

blocks.x: Getting formulas onto the sheet
A formula's job is to compute a value automatically from other cells, so that the worksheet updates itself whenever the underlying data changes.
What a formula cell actually stores

Result vs. formula When you type a formula into a cell and press Enter, the cell displays the computed result — not the formula text. The formula itself is only visible in the Formula Bar when that cell is selected, or by pressing F2 (or double-clicking the cell) to edit it in place, which highlights every cell the formula refers to.
How a formula must start
Every formula must begin with one of three symbols so the spreadsheet knows to calculate rather than treat the entry as plain text:

c: Also accepted as a formula start (habit carried over from older spreadsheets)
Formula start where the leading minus negates the first term

blocks.x: What may appear inside a formula A valid formula can combine: arithmetic operators (+, −, *, /, etc.), relational (comparison) operators (=, >, <, etc.), mathematical expressions, and built-in functions — e.g. =COS(20) calls the cosine function on the value 20.
Entering a formula

items: 1Select an empty cell — a formula can only be typed into a cell that currently holds nothing (or that you intend to overwrite).
2Type = (or + / -) followed by the expression, references and functions that make up the calculation.
3Press Enter. The cell now shows the result; the underlying formula appears in the Formula Bar whenever the cell is reselected.
4To inspect or edit the formula again, press F2 or double-click the cell — this switches the cell itself into edit mode and colour-highlights every referenced cell on the sheet.

blocks.x: Cell C2 above displays 50 (the result), while the Formula Bar for C2 shows the text =A2*B2.
The payoff: automatic recalculation

Automatic recalculation The single biggest reason to use formulas instead of typing computed numbers directly: if any cell a formula refers to changes, the formula's result updates automatically — no re-typing, no re-computing by hand. Change the Price or Qty above and Total recalculates itself instantly.
Entering references by pointing instead of typing

Rather than typing a cell address from memory, you can build a reference by pointing: type =, then click the target cell — Excel inserts its address and surrounds the cell with a moving dashed marquee border. To reference a whole range, click the first cell and drag across to the last cell; Excel inserts the range as start:end (e.g. B4:D4).

items: A formula must start with =, + or -.
The cell shows the result; the Formula Bar (or F2 / double-click) shows the formula.
Formulas can mix arithmetic operators, comparison operators, expressions and built-in functions like COS().
Formulas exist mainly so results recalculate automatically when source data changes.
References can be typed or built by pointing and dragging.

blocks.x: Copying formulas correctly
How a reference behaves when a formula is copied or filled to other cells depends entirely on whether it is relative, absolute, or mixed.
Relative references

Relative reference The default type of reference in a spreadsheet — e.g. B4. When a formula containing a relative reference is copied or filled to another cell, the reference adjusts automatically to keep the same relative position to the new cell.

If the formula in B5 — =(+B4-B3)/B2 — is filled across to column Z, every relative reference shifts by the same number of columns. Filled into Z6, it becomes =(+Z5-Z4)/Z3 — each reference has moved one row down and from column B to column Z, exactly matching the cell's new position relative to Z6.
Likewise, =SUM(B4:D4) entered in a cell and copied to F5 becomes =SUM(B5:D5) — the whole range shifts down one row to match the new cell's row.
Absolute references
Absolute reference A reference locked with the $ sign so it does not change when copied — e.g. $A$5 stays $A$5 no matter where the formula is copied to. The $ can fix the column, the row, or both.

Here $D$4 might hold a fixed tax or markup rate. Because it is absolute, copying =SUM(B4:D4)*$D$4 to any other cell keeps the multiplier anchored to D4 — it never shifts — while B4:D4 (relative) adjusts as usual.

Typing vs. toggling absolute references You can type the $ signs manually, or select the reference (in the formula) and press F4 to cycle through all four forms in order: A10 → $A$10 → A$10 → $A10 → A10.
Mixed references

Mixed reference Locks only the column or only the row. $G5 — column absolute, row relative — keeps column G fixed but lets the row adjust when copied down or across. G$5 — row absolute, column relative — keeps row 5 fixed but lets the column adjust.

c: Column A stays fixed; row adjusts

blocks.x: Example: =$A4*B$3 — column A is locked for the first factor (so it always multiplies by whatever is in column A of the current row), while row 3 is locked for the second factor (so it always multiplies by whatever is in row 3 of the current column). This pattern is exactly what you need to build a multiplication-style grid that references one fixed column of values against one fixed row of values.
Circular references

Circular reference Occurs when a formula, directly or indirectly, refers back to the very cell it is in — e.g. typing =(D1+D2-D3)/3 into cell D3 itself. Because D3 needs its own result to compute itself, the calculation can never resolve. Circular references are not permitted and should always be corrected.
Referencing other worksheets

Cross-sheet reference syntax To reference a cell on another sheet, prefix the cell address with the sheet name and an exclamation mark: Sheet5!A10 refers to cell A10 on "Sheet5". A custom-named sheet works the same way, e.g. CSM1!A10. If the sheet name contains spaces, it must be wrapped in single quotes: 'CSM 1'!A10.
3-D references

3-D reference Sums (or otherwise aggregates) the same cell or range across a span of sheets, using FirstSheet:LastSheet!Range. For example, =SUM(Sheet1:Sheet4!$D$1:$D$10) adds up cells D1:D10 on Sheet1, Sheet2, Sheet3 and Sheet4 in one formula — useful for consolidating four months' or four branches' worth of identically-laid-out data.

items: Relative (B4): adjusts automatically when copied.
Absolute ($B$4): never changes when copied — press F4 to add both $ signs.
Mixed ($B4 or B$4): locks only the column or only the row.
Never let a formula refer back to its own cell — that's a circular reference.
Other sheets: Sheet5!A10, or 'CSM 1'!A10 for a name with a space.
3-D references aggregate the same range across a run of sheets: Sheet1:Sheet4!$D$1:$D$10.

blocks.x: The four operator families
Operators specify what calculation to perform; precedence rules decide which operation happens first when several appear in one formula.
The four operator types

items: 1Arithmetic operators — perform basic mathematical operations and return numbers.
2Comparison (relational) operators — compare two values and return the logical value TRUE or FALSE.
3Text concatenation operator — joins two text values into one.
4Reference operators — combine ranges of cells for calculations.

blocks.x: Arithmetic operators

c: Subtraction, or negation when used alone

blocks.x: Comparison operators
Text concatenation operator
& (ampersand) Joins ("concatenates") two text strings into a single string. For example, ="CSM"&"183" produces the text "CSM183".
Reference operators

c: Produces one reference to all cells between two references, inclusive
Combines multiple references into one, non-contiguous, reference
Produces a reference to cells common to both ranges; returns #NULL! if the ranges share no cells

blocks.x: What gets calculated first

When a formula mixes several operators, the spreadsheet evaluates them in a fixed order, from highest to lowest precedence: negation, then percent, then exponentiation, then multiplication/division (left to right), then addition/subtraction (left to right). Parentheses always override this default order — whatever is inside them is evaluated first.
( ) Parentheses→ – Negation→ % Percent→ ^ Exponent→ * / (L→R)→ + – (L→R)
Full precedence, highest to lowest: reference operators → negation → percent → exponent → multiplication/division → addition/subtraction → concatenation (&) → comparison.
Parentheses change everything
How operator evaluation is governed
Rule 1 — Higher precedence is evaluated first When operators of different precedence appear together, the one higher in the order is calculated first.
Rule 2 — Equal precedence is evaluated left to right When two or more operators share the same precedence level (like * and /, or + and −), the calculation proceeds strictly from left to right.
Rule 3 — Parentheses force a different order Anything enclosed in parentheses is calculated first, regardless of the default precedence — this is how you override the built-in order.

items: Four categories: arithmetic, comparison, text concatenation (&), reference (: , space).
Comparison operators always return TRUE or FALSE.
Precedence, high to low: reference ops → negation → % → ^ → */ → +- → & → comparison.
Rule 1: higher precedence first — 8/2^3 = 1.
Rule 2: equal precedence goes left to right — 10/5*2 = 4.
Rule 3: parentheses override everything — 10/(5*2) = 1.

sections.title: What a valid name must look like

blocks.x: Readable, maintainable formulas
Instead of remembering that sales figures live in B2:B12, give the range a name — like Sales — and use that name in formulas instead.

Why name a cell or range?
A name is a meaningful shorthand for a cell or range address. =SUM(Sales) is easier to read, write and audit than =SUM(B2:B12), and the name still works correctly even if rows are inserted above the range.
What a valid name must look like

items: 1Must start with a letter or an underscore ( _ ) — it cannot start with a number or a symbol other than underscore.
2Cannot contain spaces or hyphens — use an underscore or capitalisation instead, e.g. Unit_Price or UnitPrice.
3Can be at most 255 characters long.
4Names are not case-sensitive — Sales, SALES and sales all refer to the same defined name.

blocks.x: Defining a name via the Name Box

Select the cell or range you want to name, click into the Name Box at the top-left of the worksheet (where the active cell's address normally shows), type the name, and press Enter. This is the fastest way to define a single name.
Defining a name via the Formulas tab
Select the range, go to Formulas tab → Define Name, which opens the New Name dialog with three fields:

c: The name you are assigning, following the naming rules above
An optional note describing what the name represents
The cell or range address the name points to — pre-filled from your selection, but editable

blocks.x: The Name Manager

Name Manager Found on the Formulas tab, the Name Manager lists every defined name in the workbook and lets you create, edit or delete several names in one session — useful when a worksheet needs many named ranges rather than defining them one at a time.

items: Naming rules: start with a letter/underscore, no spaces or hyphens, max 255 characters, not case-sensitive.
Fastest way to name one range: type the name directly into the Name Box.
Formulas tab → Define Name opens the New Name dialog: Name, Comment, Refers To.
Name Manager (Formulas tab) is the tool for creating/editing several names in one session.
